analysis.one_liner: Eases federal nursing home rules for states while capping what facilities can charge Medicaid residents.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote of its own: introduced with zero cosponsors, it sat in committee for four months until its provisions were folded into a larger year-end bill (H.R. 5835) on November 5, 1990.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would revise the 1987 nursing home reform rules attached to Medicaid, the federal-state health program for low-income people. It would shield states from federal penalties for falling short on nurse aide training and preadmission screening if they made a good-faith effort, create exceptions to screening for certain hospital discharges, and delay screening for private-pay residents. At the same time, it would add real protections for residents: facilities could not bill Medicaid-eligible residents above the state's Medicaid payment rate, residents could refuse certain room transfers and see their clinical records, and inspection results would have to be made public within 14 days.
analysis.who_benefits: Two groups gain. Medicaid nursing home residents get a hard cap: a facility cannot charge a Medicaid-eligible resident more than the state's Medicaid payment amount, even when the resident's own income exceeds that amount [S3]. Residents also gain the right to refuse transfers into a facility's Medicare-certified wing, prompt access to their clinical records, and public disclosure of inspection results within 14 days [S3]. States and nursing facilities get the other half of the bargain: relief from federal sanctions during a grace period, screening exemptions for certain hospital discharges, delayed screening for private-pay residents, a longer window (4 to 14 days) to complete resident assessments, and a 90-day grace period for temporary nurse aides [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicaid nursing home residents, states, and nursing facilities

how_it_helps.text: Caps what nursing facilities can charge Medicaid-eligible residents at the state's Medicaid payment amounts, closing a gap where residents whose income exceeded the Medicaid rate could be billed the difference [S3].
Bars federal action against states that made a good-faith effort to meet the 1987 nurse aide training and preadmission screening requirements before federal guidelines took effect [S3].

Exempts certain direct hospital discharges (short stays under 30 days certified by a physician) from preadmission screening, and delays screening and annual review for residents who are not on Medicaid at admission [S3].

Gives residents the right to refuse a room transfer aimed at moving them into a facility's Medicare-qualified portion, prompt access to their clinical records, and guarantees public disclosure of survey results within 14 days [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Nursing facilities bear the cost of the charge cap, since they can no longer bill Medicaid-eligible residents above the state payment amount [S3]. They and states also take on new annual reporting on screened residents [S3]. Weaker screening means some people who do not need nursing-home-level care could be admitted, and the federal program would be barred from paying for residents who do not require that level of services [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Nursing facilities and, for skipped screenings, some residents

drawbacks.text: The bill loosens the preadmission screening system that OBRA 1987 created to keep people who do not need nursing facility care out of those facilities and to review mentally ill and mentally retarded residents; it waives penalties for past state noncompliance and lets states skip screening for private-pay residents until they become Medicaid-eligible [S3].
Extending the resident assessment window from 4 days to 14 days delays the comprehensive evaluation that triggers each resident's care plan [S3].
Shielding states from federal sanctions for missed nurse aide training and screening deadlines, even on a good-faith basis, removes one of the levers that forces compliance with care standards [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a genuine two-way trade: its charge cap, records access, and disclosure rules are real protections for a vulnerable population, while its screening exemptions and penalty forbearance water down the 1987 reform's front-line safeguards. The clearest loss is that preadmission screening — the tool for keeping people out of nursing homes who do not need them — becomes optional for private-pay residents and skipped for many hospital discharges. Weighing it honestly, the resident protections are concrete and enforceable, but the relief provisions tilt the balance toward facility and state convenience.

outcome.mechanism: The bill never came to a vote of its own; it sat in committee from July until November 5, 1990, when its provisions were rolled into the larger year-end budget bill H.R. 5835, and the standalone bill died there.

narrative.text: Gerry Sikorski introduced the bill on July 10, 1990, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce; no one else signed on as a cosponsor [S1].
On July 27, 1990, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment, where it remained without action for over three months [S5].
On November 5, 1990, the record notes that its provisions were included in H.R. 5835, the large year-end budget package; the standalone bill itself never received a vote in either chamber [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never stood on its own, the record shows no public debate or vote on any of its provisions — they either traveled quietly inside the year-end package or disappeared with it. The clearest beneficiary of that path was the nursing home industry, since the bill's relief provisions (penalty forbearance, screening exemptions, longer deadlines) could take effect without a standalone fight, while its charge cap on facilities rode along in the same package.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nursing homes, via quiet inclusion in the year-end package

for.name: Rep. Gerry E. Sikorski
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Medicaid Nursing Home Reform Act of 1990 on July 10, 1990

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment on July 27, 1990, and never reported it out; the bill died in committee

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had zero cosponsors, so there is no record of where either party stood; it was the work of a single House Democrat.

industries.industry: Nursing homes and long-term care facilities
industries.note: The bill hands facilities relief from the 1987 reform: federal penalty forbearance, screening exemptions for hospital discharges and private-pay residents, a longer assessment window, and a grace period for temporary nurse aides. But it also bars facilities from charging Medicaid-eligible residents more than the state's Medicaid payment amount — a real revenue limit — and adds public disclosure of inspection results.

States gain protection from federal sanctions while making a good-faith effort on nurse aide training and screening, plus screening exemptions and deadline relief. They take on new annual reporting on screened residents and cannot delegate screening duties to the nursing facilities themselves.
